summary: A description of the choices BBN made when implementing the host-host protocol, the initial connection protocol and Telnet on the Terminal IMP. The machine had very little memory and had to drive many different terminals, so some protocol options were chosen to save space and some behaviors do not fully comply with the specifications.

plainLanguage.summary: This report describes how the Terminal IMP implemented network protocols with limited memory and buffers. It lists both the features it supported and behaviors it simplified or did not guarantee.

questions: what protocols did the terminal imp implement
what were the terminal imp limitations
why did the terminal imp ignore some commands
subtitle: How a Terminal IMP implemented NCP, ICP and TELNET under tight resource limits.

tldr.problem: A Terminal IMP had little memory, no bulk storage and had to serve many terminals, so it could not implement every protocol behavior without limits.
tldr.mechanism: The report documents choices and deviations in its NCP, ICP and TELNET implementation, including buffer, timeout and command-handling limits.
tldr.outcome: It explains why the implementation made these trade-offs and records areas of non-compliance for network users and implementers.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 215 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The document reports implementation choices and deviations for a Terminal IMP.

sections.title: The Terminal IMP's Constraints
sections.content:
The Terminal IMP was built to give network access to up to 64 terminals, not to provide service to other hosts. It had no bulk storage and 8K of 16-bit words for device I/O buffers and programs. It needed to support as many as 128 simplex network connections.

The implementation described includes NCP, ICP and TELNET. The report says data-transfer protocol support was expected later, but the portions to implement had not been clearly defined.
sections.plainLanguage: The Terminal IMP connected many terminals to the network but had limited memory and no bulk storage. Its programmers had to choose which protocol functions to support.

sections.title: Documented Deviations
sections.content:
The Terminal IMP does not guarantee a response to every ECO command, and it may discard unsolicited RFCs. After sending CLS, it waits a limited time for a matching CLS before freeing the connection's sockets. It ignores RET commands to avoid a possible rapid RET-ALL loop and ignores GVB commands because implementation would require many instructions.

These are stated implementation choices, not general protocol rules. The RFC gives the reasons in terms of buffering, memory and processing limits.
sections.plainLanguage: Some control requests may be ignored or receive no guaranteed reply. The report explains these limits as choices made to fit the Terminal IMP's resources.

sections.title: Allocation and Connection Handling
sections.content:
The Terminal IMP allocates limited buffering for each receiving connection and issues a new allocation when buffers empty and allocation remains below the maximum. A total bit allocation above 65,534 is treated as infinite to keep the value in a single word.

For ICP, it ignores the 32-bit socket number received over the logger connection and accepts the first RTS and STR from the specified host for the user's sockets. Its socket numbers are preassigned using the terminal's physical address. The implementation also follows the ICP Listen option when acting as the user site.
sections.plainLanguage: The system keeps allocation data small and uses preassigned socket numbers. During connection setup, it accepts the first matching requests from the selected host.

sections.title: Input Checks and Reported Limits
sections.content:
The Terminal IMP assumes incoming messages follow the relevant protocols but checks some limits. It discards control messages longer than 120 bytes, stops processing a control message if it encounters an opcode greater than 13, and discards data that exceeds the assumed bit allocation.

The RFC records these behaviors so users understand how the implementation differs from the full protocol descriptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The Terminal IMP checks some message sizes and codes, but it assumes other incoming data is already valid. The report documents these limits for people communicating with it.

references.text: RFC 202, cited in the discussion of ICP deadlock.
